transcript.text: My Beko keeps stopping randomly in the middle of a wash with water still in it. Sometimes it's fine for a week, then it does it twice in a day. The model starts WTG I think. I've cleaned the filter. Driving me mad.

With water left in the drum despite a clean filter, the leading possibility is an intermittent drain fault: a partially obstructed pump/hosing, a failing drain pump, or its connection. A clean filter does not completely rule those out. If it is instead sitting in the main wash phase while still tumbling, a heating fault becomes more likely; if it drains but then behaves as though water remains, level sensing is another possibility. When it stops, is it usually near the end/before spin or genuinely during the washing/tumbling part — and can you hear a humming or buzzing as though it is trying to pump the water out? That distinction is the useful one: pump noise with no drain points towards the pump or a restriction after the filter; no attempt to drain points more towards its wiring/control or a different stage-related fault. Switch off and unplug it before doing any further filter or hose checks, and have towels ready if water needs draining.

It stops during the wash itself, not at the end - water's in the drum and the display just freezes. Nothing odd beforehand, no humming or buzzing that I've noticed, though the pump does sometimes run briefly then stop. Sometimes if I switch it off and on it carries on and finishes, other times it stalls again.

Because it freezes during the washing part rather than when it should be emptying, the brief pump activity is less convincing for a simple blocked-drain fault. A clean filter also makes that less likely, though not impossible. The two main possibilities now are:
1. An intermittent heating fault — usually the heater, temperature sensor or a connection. This commonly shows up after the machine has been washing for a while and is trying to heat the water.
2. An intermittent control-side fault — such as a door-lock, wiring connection or control module issue. The fact that switching off and back on can sometimes let it continue supports this, but does not prove the module itself is bad. The useful no-tools comparison is to try a cold or 30°C quick wash, then compare it with a 40°C-or-hotter programme. Does it stall on both, or only/reliably on the warmer programme? Also note whether an error code appears when the display freezes. If cold cycles complete but heated ones stall, the heating circuit becomes the leading suspect and an engineer should test it safely with the machine isolated. If it happens equally on cold cycles with no pattern, the door-lock/wiring/control side moves ahead. Avoid repeatedly restarting it with water inside if it is becoming frequent; use the drain/spin programme first if it will respond, and unplug it before any filter or hose work.
It does it on cold washes too, so not just the hot ones. No error code that I can make out, just the time freezing and sometimes a flashing light I think is the start light. What do you reckon then?

My best call now is an intermittent door-lock feedback fault, its wiring connection, or—secondarily—the control module. It is much less likely to be the heater because it also happens on cold washes, and less like a straightforward drain blockage because it stops during washing rather than at the emptying stage. The flashing Start light is the useful clue: it can indicate the machine believes it is paused or has lost the confirmation that the door is safely locked. Cycling the power sometimes getting it going again also fits an intermittent lock/contact or control issue, but does not prove the control board is at fault. 1. When it next freezes, press Start/Pause once and wait briefly. Note whether it carries on or simply remains frozen.
2. Also check whether the door is still locked at that point. Do not force it. If one press resumes it, or the door-lock status changes unexpectedly, the door-lock assembly or its wiring becomes the leading suspect. If it remains locked and powered but completely ignores Start/Pause, an engineer should investigate the internal wiring and control module before any part is chosen. Avoid leaving it running unattended until it is sorted; stop using it if there is any burning smell, heat around the controls, or signs of water leaking.

Right, I haven't tried pressing Start/Pause when it's frozen, I just switch it off and on. I can try that next time it stalls. Not sure how to check the door lock though, do you mean just try opening it? It's out of warranty too, so I don't want to pay for an engineer unless I have to.
AI service unavailable. Please try again in a moment.

Sorry, I think your last message didn't come through, it just said the service was unavailable. I asked how to check the door lock, do you just mean try opening it when it's frozen? I'll try pressing Start/Pause next time it stalls.

Not as a test by forcing it open. With water still in the drum, the door should normally remain locked; that is a safety function and does not, by itself, prove the door lock is faulty. Do not pull hard on the handle or try to defeat the lock. When it freezes, press Start/Pause once and give it about a minute. Note whether it resumes, simply stays frozen, or changes to a paused state. Then try the handle only normally and gently: if it remains locked, leave it alone. If one press reliably gets it going again, that points more towards an intermittent control/door-feedback connection than a blocked pump. If it stays locked and ignores Start/Pause while the display is frozen, an engineer should test the door interlock wiring, water-level sensing and control board connections before anyone condemns a part. A clean filter and the fact it happens on cold washes make a heater fault less likely, but do not yet prove a door-lock fault. Given it is intermittent and can leave water in the drum, I would avoid unattended washes until it is diagnosed.

Ok, thanks, I won't force it. I'll try pressing Start/Pause next time it stalls and see what happens. If that doesn't work, is there anything else I can check myself before paying for an engineer? I'm not going to take any panels off though.

Yes — without removing panels, there are two worthwhile checks before paying for a visit. 1. With it switched off and unplugged, pull it forward enough to inspect the drain hose all the way to the waste pipe. Make sure it is not kinked, crushed behind the machine, or sealed tightly/pushed excessively far into the standpipe. A hose restriction can be intermittent and a clean filter does not rule it out. 2. Check the door closes squarely and clicks shut without having to lift, push or hold it. Look only at the visible catch and door alignment; do not dismantle or force anything. If its behaviour changes when the door is gently pushed inward, that supports a catch/interlock alignment or connection issue. The next useful test remains Start/Pause when it freezes. If it resumes after one press, the stronger suspects are an intermittent control/connection issue or a false pause condition. If it ignores Start/Pause and remains frozen, an engineer will need to test the internal wiring, water-level sensor system and control electronics — none can be properly confirmed from outside without removing panels. An independent appliance engineer should diagnose it rather than replacing parts by guesswork.
